questions.text: In the GMP model, what are G, M, and P?
options: G goroutine, M OS thread, P logical processor (queue/quota)
G GC, M mutex, P panic
G global heap, M malloc, P page

questions.text: Why does the Go scheduler use work stealing?
options: An idle P takes goroutines from another P’s queue
So every goroutine lives on one M

questions.text: What is async preemption in Go (since 1.14)?
options: A goroutine is preempted only at a function call
The scheduler waits for an explicit Gosched
A goroutine can be preempted even in a tight loop, not only at call/syscall

questions.text: What does runtime.LockOSThread do?
options: Holds the scheduler mutex until main ends
Binds the current goroutine to this OS thread until UnlockOSThread

questions.text: Does a goroutine have a stable id in the language?
options: No public id: the language does not give one (only debug tricks)
Yes, it is the OS thread number

questions.text: Why are thousands of goroutines usually cheaper than thousands of OS threads?
options: Small growable stacks and a user scheduler, not a full kernel context each

questions.text: Why does the runtime have a sysmon thread?
options: It is the only thread that runs main
Background monitoring: long syscalls, preemption, timers

questions.text: Why is a cgo call often more expensive than ordinary goroutine work?
options: cgo is forbidden together with go
The compiler rejects mixing C and Go
It must enter a thread that can call C, which breaks cheap G switching

questions.text: The language spec gives a goroutine a stable numeric id.
Work stealing lets an idle P take work from another P’s queue.
Since Go 1.14 a tight loop with no calls need not spin forever without preemption.
LockOSThread pins the goroutine to the current OS thread.
P in GMP is an operating-system thread.
Creating a goroutine is usually more expensive than creating an OS thread.
M in GMP is an OS thread that can run Go code.
The Go scheduler guarantees fairness: every goroutine gets CPU in a fixed quantum.
What are G, M, and P in the Go scheduler?
questions.answer: G goroutine, M OS thread, P the resource/queue for running Go code.

questions.text: What is scheduler work stealing?
questions.answer: An idle P takes goroutines from another P’s queue (or the global one).

questions.text: What did async preemption (Go 1.14) change?
questions.answer: A goroutine can be preempted without a function call, including in a tight loop.

questions.text: What does runtime.LockOSThread do?
questions.answer: Pins the current goroutine to the current OS thread until UnlockOSThread.

questions.text: Does a goroutine have an id in the language?
Why are goroutines cheaper than OS threads?
questions.answer: Small growable stacks and a user-space scheduler, not a full kernel context each.

questions.text: Why does the runtime have sysmon?
questions.answer: Background: long syscalls, preemption, timers, and scheduler health.

questions.text: Why is cgo more expensive than ordinary goroutine switching?
questions.answer: A thread that can call C is required; cheap G switching breaks down there.
